extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of political economy, social reformers, and policy‑makers interested in remedies for poverty and land reform
extracted.subtask_description: A set of normative criteria and tests for assessing proposed remedies to poverty and the unequal distribution of wealth, especially those addressing land ownership. Emphasizes justice, practicality, conformity with social development, and effects on production and incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedy must remove the cause, not merely symptoms
rubrics_metrics.description: There is but one way to remove an evil—and that is, to remove its cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test proposed measures by whether they attack the underlying cause of poverty (private property in land). Measures that only mitigate symptoms (temporary relief, palliatives) are inadequate. The sufficiency of a remedy should be judged by whether it directly addresses the primary causal mechanism identified in the analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedy must be consistent with justice (ethical test)
rubrics_metrics.description: If our inquiry is correct, the remedy must translate from political economy into terms of ethics; the remedy must be just.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an ethical test: a correct social/economic diagnosis and cure should stand when reformulated as a question of right and wrong. If a proposed remedy cannot be defended as just, it fails the ultimate test even if it seems expedient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedy must be practicable of application
rubrics_metrics.description: The remedy must be practicable of application and not merely a theoretic good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate feasibility and the ability to implement a proposal in existing social and governmental structures. The author intends to meet practical objections and demonstrate how the proposed change could be applied in reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedy must accord with tendencies of social development
rubrics_metrics.description: It must accord with the tendencies of social development and harmonize with other reforms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer reforms that 'swim with the current' of social and technological change (e.g., concentration, urbanization, industrial organization). Measures that run counter to broad historical/technological trends are likely to fail or cause harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid substituting governmental direction and restriction for individual freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever savors of regulation and restriction is in itself bad, and should not be resorted to if any other mode of accomplishing the same end presents itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies should not replace individual action with heavy-handed government control when less restrictive, freedom‑preserving means can achieve the same goal. Critical examples cited include socialistic schemes and heavy regulatory systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid measures that create inquisitorial bureaucracy and perverse incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures such as a graduated income tax would employ many officials with inquisitorial powers, create temptations to bribery and perjury, and put a premium upon unscrupulousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess proposals for institutional side effects: increased corruption, evasion, demoralization of public opinion, and burdens on conscience. A policy that systematically produces such outcomes is judged severely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not adopt measures that lessen incentives to productive accumulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Just in proportion as a tax or restriction accomplishes its effect, a lessening in the incentive to the accumulation of wealth, which is one of the strong forces of industrial progress, will occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how a proposal affects incentives to save, invest, and innovate. Measures that significantly blunt productive incentives risk reducing long‑term growth and should be rejected or redesigned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid measures that reduce aggregate production or productiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: If land in large bodies can be cultivated more cheaply than in small bodies, to restrict ownership to small bodies will reduce the aggregate production of wealth and diminish the general productiveness of labor and capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine the impact on economies of scale and total output. Reforms that would lower aggregate production (even if they redistribute ownership) may leave less to be shared and thus be counterproductive.

rubrics_metrics.name: A remedy must directly reduce economic rent to raise wages
rubrics_metrics.description: The device of restricting ownership will not reduce rent, and therefore cannot increase wages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge measures by whether they affect economic rent (the unearned income from land). Policies that fail to lower rent cannot be expected to improve the condition of laborers or raise wages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of redistributions that only create new privileged classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures like tenant‑right or minute subdivision may carve out new proprietors from landlords but do not improve the condition of the laboring class as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess who actually benefits: reforms that simply transfer property to a broader class without altering the fundamental relation (non‑producers extracting rent) preserve injustices and can entrench the system by creating more vested interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mitigations that preclude adoption of more complete cures
rubrics_metrics.description: The subdivision of land can prevent the adoption or even advocacy of more thorough-going measures, strengthening the existing unjust system by interesting a larger number in its maintenance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether modest reforms reduce political will or remove pressure for structural change. Policies that create a 'rampart' of interests against further reform can be counterproductive in the long run.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy critiques should consider historical and institutional provenance of titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Land titles rest on force, conquest, grants, and historical transfers rather than a natural right to exclusive possession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing claims of legitimacy, examine the historical basis of property rights. Titles founded on force do not constitute an absolute ethical defense against annulment by the people.
